## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why5: It keeps my audience as reservation agents and leaks nothing of Codyco's product or roles into the choice.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how agents answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words a founder reads at once; 'Contacts page' and 'open link' are Keel's own UI and clear in context.
screens.why3: I know whether I have reservation agents by name (from our 7 hotel groups and the Munich hotel) or need to post in a hotel-staff group.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my cases, but the first and third switch to 'I' while the second speaks of 'you', and the open-link one's Google sign-in is a detail a German front-desk agent might balk at that the option doesn't flag as a cost.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco's product or roles leaks; it is about distribution only and my pick (people by name) is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People I found with Keel (pick a list from Contacts; I send each link) / A group, with one open link (I post it where reservation agents already are; each signs in with Google first)

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title and "4 beliefs: 4 holding · 7 people answered" is right beside it, with each card's count against its bar, so I know the verdict and what decides it.
screens.why_b2: Prevalence, Frequency and Current solution read at once (7 of 7 said yes, bar 6 of 7), but the Importance card prints "6 of 7 put it in their two" twice, which made me look again to see if I was missing a second number.
screens.why_b3: The statement is my launch wording (5% missed, after hours, peak, holidays, seven-figure rounding error), but the Importance belief pastes my whole circumstance into a clumsy sentence, and Current solution's 'a call that came in at a busy time' is Keel's phrasing, not mine, though I still recognise both.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what all four holding means for Codyco, such as whether to move on to the solution stage or take this to hotel-group directors, and the only line at the bottom explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown on every card, but nobody says that seven agents is a small sample, and the verdict sits directly under my 5% and seven-figure claim as if the answers confirmed those numbers, when no card measured either.
screens.instead: Holding up across all four beliefs from 7 reservation agents, a small sample: the missed booking call is common, frequent and a top pain, but my 5% and seven-figure figures were not tested here, so next check the size of the loss with revenue directors.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I can see my belief held and the count that decides it.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells, all for me, on an axis from 0 to 7, with the marker at 6 labelled with my at least 8 in 10: I can see what is counted, over how many people and where my bar is.
screens.why_b3: My band, At least 8 in 10, is mine and the missed booking call is my problem, but the belief says 'reservation agents' and drops 'at hotel groups' with a central office or call center, which is the group I actually sell to.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' only sends me to the next two cards; it does not say what this result means for selling to hotel groups, such as that missed calls are not just my claim and the real question is how many and what they cost.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the card says plainly that 7 is a small group, 'a lean, not a call', so it claims nothing the seven answers cannot carry.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 reservation agents at hotel groups let a booking call ring out unanswered in the last 7 days: all 7 of 7 said yes, above your bar of 6. That is a lean from a small group, so the pitch should rest on how many calls ring out and what they cost, which the next two cards show.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside median 6 days out of 7 and 6 of 7 inside my 5 to 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7, the 7 people and the marker at 5 are plain, but the legend's 'what you said' next to 'at what you said' made me look twice to tell the band from the cells inside it.
screens.why_b3: Frequency is my dimension and 5 to 7 days is my range, but 'reservation agents let a booking call ring out' makes it sound like my agents drop calls, when my point is that calls after hours, at peak and on holidays go unanswered whoever is on shift.
screens.why_b4: '6 of 7 sit in your band. Whether it matters is the next card' repeats the count and points onward, but never says what a near-daily miss means for my pitch to a reservations director.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and 'a lean, not a call' are said honestly, but the asked line's tag 'the most recent time it happened' misdescribes a question that counted days over the whole week.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean from 7 agents: 6 of 7 had an unanswered booking call on 5 or more of the last 7 days (middle answer 6), so missed calls are near-daily, not an after-hours edge case; next, see whether directors price that loss.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7", so I know it held and by how much; the line is printed twice, but that is clutter, not a contradiction.
screens.why_b2: The caption says the bars count 14 picks from 7 people who each picked two, my row is marked with 6, and the strip shows one cell per person with the marker at 5 of 7, so the count, the n and the bar are all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise it, but my row was answering every booking call before it rings out, and "that rings" drops the missed call I am actually selling against; the belief also loses "at hotel groups" and is missing a comma before "and not every one gets answered".
screens.why_b4: The So line only cautions that top two is not first place; it never tells me what 6 of 7 means for Codyco, or that the one against is a group whose call center already covers after hours, which is exactly the segment I need to qualify.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said outright, the claim is limited to these 7, and nothing calls the result strong.
screens.instead: Holding up, 6 of 7 put answering every booking call before it rings out in their two (bar 5 of 7, a lean from 7). The one against has a call center covering after hours and is busier with group emails, so check whether a group already has night cover before you pitch it.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', and the chart, strip and names all add up to the same 6 for and 1 against (Chiara).
screens.why_b2: The five rungs with their counts, the line under 'A few rang out, all called back that day', the for/against labels and the strip marker at 5 of 7 are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Current solution and 'still falls short' are mine, but 'a booking call that came in at a busy time' narrows my after hours, peak and holidays to just busy times, and the stem's 'your last booking call' (one call) does not match rungs that count many calls ringing out.
screens.why_b4: The So line breaks the gap down rung by rung, but 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is generic; it does not say that the 4 whose rung-out calls were lost or barely called back are exactly the bookings Codyco recovers.
screens.why_b5: n = 7 stays visible, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is said outright, and nothing is called stronger than 6 of 7 carries.
screens.instead: Ask about my last shift's calls, after hours, at peak or on a holiday, not 'your last booking call'; then say: 4 of 7 lost most rung-out calls outright, and those are the bookings forwarding to Codyco would recover, so test that first.

screens.why_b1: The line opens on "Holding up" and says "Importance held, 6 of 7" right beside the bar of 5 of 7, so I have both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: Importance is the dimension I checked, and the belief line is my circumstance and my "answering every booking call that rings", so it reads as mine.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what Chiara's answer means for Codyco, for example whether to drop groups whose call center already covers after six from the segment, or whether group requests and emails are a pain worth watching.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible (1 against, 1 asked, a group of 1), and nothing grows one person's answer into a trend.
screens.why_b6: Chiara gives me what I did not type: where a call center already answers after six, the missed call stops being the pain and unrated group emails take its place, which is a boundary on my segment.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I am the person the study wants, and I am: I take booking calls in our group's central reservations office in Munich.
screens.why2: 'Central reservations office' and 'call centre' are the words we use for my workplace, so I can answer at once.
screens.why3: Where I work is the one thing I know for certain.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with nothing missing, and a gate question needs no escape.
screens.why5: It names the founder's segment in plain trade words, and nothing about a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options I can hold after hearing it once; the 'I'll read 2 options' lead-in is a little stiff for a plain yes-or-no but easy to follow.

screens.why1: Right after I said I work in a central reservations office, asking whether calls went unanswered this week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Ring out' I understand, but 'let' sounds like I chose to ignore it; on the floor we say a caller dropped out of the queue or hung up before we picked up.
screens.why3: In our office the calls sit in the queue and people hang up there, so on a trade-fair Saturday I rarely see one particular call ring out on my own phone; I would half guess from the queue board.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the two chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product reaches me, but 'let it ring out' turns the office's missed calls into my own fault, so an agent who was busy on another line might truthfully say No.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'Yes or no' at the end, easy to answer once heard.
screens.why7: The gate has the two fixed answers in order and no escape, it names the window and the missed call rather than the routine of taking calls, and both Yes and No are true of someone, so the belief can be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a guest hang up on a booking call before you could answer? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to having calls ring out, asking on how many days it happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'Ring out unanswered' and 'booking call' are how we talk on the reservations floor; I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: In our central office the calls sit in the queue, and on a trade-fair Saturday I see abandoned calls on the wallboard rather than a phone I personally 'let' ring, so I'd half-guess what counts as mine.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 plus 'I can't recall' covers every true answer with no overlap.
screens.why5: The idea that not every call gets answered is kept, but 'you let' turns it into my personal failing when it's usually the queue at peak.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold.
screens.why7: One measure in days of the window, buttons 1 to 7 in order with no 0 or bands, the unit said once, and 'I can't recall' as the only escape, so the founder's range can be read against it.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did a booking call go unanswered on your shift? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking how often I let calls ring out, it makes sense to ask which hard part of my shift I'd most want eased.
screens.why2: These are the words of my office: booking emails, group requests, rates on every channel, changes to bookings; I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: Most rows are my own shift's work, though keeping rates right on every channel is more revenue management's job than mine in our central office.
screens.why4: 'Booking emails and group requests' is two things in one row, and the rates row belongs to another desk, so one option is odd even though the true answer is there.
screens.why5: Answering every booking call that rings keeps the founder's 'every caller' aim in my words, and nothing of a product leaks to me.
screens.why6: One short question and five short options I can hold, with 'none of these' said last; only the emails-and-group-requests row is a little long.
screens.why7: The founder's own row is there and not first, and the escape is right, but one row packs two tasks and another is someone else's job, so the shape rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift with calls coming in. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Answering booking emails · Handling changes to existing bookings · Answering every booking call that rings · Handling group requests · Answering guests' questions about their stay · None of these

screens.why1: After the screens about calls ringing out, it makes sense to ask how well my office copes with busy-time calls today and what happens to the ones we miss.
screens.why2: "Answering a booking call that came in at a busy time" right after "your last booking call" made me read it twice, because I wasn't sure if they meant one call or a whole rush.
screens.why3: I know how my last Saturday rush went, but my last single call I simply answered, so I'd have to guess they mean the shift and answer for that instead.
screens.why4: The stem asks about one call, but the options count how many rang out and how many we called back, so no option fits one call; each option also packs two things together (how many rang out, and the callback), and "called back when there was time" overlaps with "few were called back".
screens.why5: Booking calls ringing out and calling back are my own words, and nothing of anyone's product comes through.
screens.why6: The stem says "booking call" twice and its second half is a mouthful to hear, though the five options themselves are short enough to hold.
screens.why7: There are five options in order, the first works and the last fails outright, the belief could go either way, and the escape is there; but the options don't answer the stem's single occasion, and each mixes how many rang out with whether they were called back.
screens.instead: Think of your last busy shift. What happened to the booking calls you couldn't pick up? Every call answered live · A few rang out, all called back that day · Some rang out, a few never called back · Many rang out, most never called back · Missed calls were simply lost; or: Someone else took the calls
